questions.passage: The two brothers had not spoken in eleven years. When their father died, they met in the lawyer's office — the first time since the argument neither of them could fully remember starting. Thomas sat with his hands in his lap. David kept his coat on, as though he might need to leave quickly. The lawyer read the will, which left everything equally to both of them, including the lake house where they had spent every summer of their childhood. Thomas looked at his brother. David looked at the window. 'We could sell it,' David said finally. 'Or,' Thomas said slowly, 'we could go there.'
questions.text: Which TWO details from the passage most strongly support the inference that neither brother truly wants to sever their connection?
options: They met in a lawyer's office after eleven years of silence, and David kept his coat on
Thomas looked at his brother rather than away, and Thomas suggests going to the lake house instead of selling
The argument that caused the rift is described as one 'neither could fully remember starting,' and the will divides everything equally
David suggests selling the lake house, and the lawyer reads the will aloud
questions.explanation: Thomas making eye contact with his brother and offering to go to the lake house — rather than agreeing to sell — are the two details that most directly signal his reluctance to cut ties completely.

questions.passage: Rosa had been the fastest runner in her grade for three years straight. When a new student, Aaliyah, arrived and finished the mile run two seconds faster, Rosa refused to race her again. She told herself she was 'resting her ankle.' She avoided the track during lunch and began arriving late to PE. One afternoon, the coach pulled her aside. 'I've watched a lot of runners,' he said. 'The ones who quit when they lose are the ones who stop getting better.' Rosa didn't answer him. But the next morning, she was at the track before the sun came up.
questions.text: What theme does this story develop, and how is it conveyed?
options: Natural talent is more important than hard work, conveyed through Rosa's innate speed
Competition can be destructive, conveyed through Rosa's avoidance of Aaliyah
Growth requires facing failure rather than avoiding it, conveyed through Rosa's eventual return to training
Coaches understand athletes better than athletes understand themselves, conveyed through the coach's speech
questions.explanation: The coach's direct statement and Rosa's return to the track before sunrise show the story's theme: avoiding defeat prevents growth, while facing it drives improvement.

questions.passage: The village of Kestrel Hollow sat at the edge of a forest that the oldest residents said was haunted. Nobody went in after dark — not because of any rule, but because of the boy who had gone in forty years ago and come out different. He was still there, old now, keeping bees at the forest's edge. When the drought came, his bees were the only ones that continued to thrive. The farmers began leaving offerings at the edge of his property: jars of honey, dried flowers, small coins. He never acknowledged them. But the jars were always empty by morning.
questions.text: How do the setting and the beekeeper character interact to create the story's atmosphere?
options: The forest setting makes the beekeeper seem dangerous, and his silence confirms he is a villain
The haunted forest and the beekeeper's mysterious past combine to create an atmosphere of quiet, unsettling strangeness
The drought creates conflict between the beekeeper and the farmers, driving the story's plot
The village setting contrasts with the forest to show that civilization is safer than nature
questions.explanation: The combination of the reputedly haunted forest, the beekeeper's unexplained transformation, his silence, and the mysteriously emptied jars work together to produce an atmosphere of eerie, low-key strangeness.

questions.passage: The poem repeats the refrain 'nothing gold can stay' at the end of each stanza, describing dawn turning to day, flowers fading, and, finally, Eden's loss of innocence. The gold of dawn does not last; neither does the gold of youth.
questions.text: What is the effect of repeating the refrain 'nothing gold can stay' across the stanzas?
options: It creates a sense of escalating joy as each stanza introduces a new golden image
It reinforces the theme that beauty and innocence are fleeting, building a sense of inevitable loss
It confuses the reader by applying the same line to unrelated subjects
It emphasizes the literal value of gold as a symbol of wealth throughout history
questions.explanation: Each repetition of the refrain caps a new example of something precious and temporary, accumulating emotional weight and driving home the poem's central theme of inevitable loss.

questions.passage: The story alternates between two characters trapped in an elevator: Nadia, a surgeon who has already missed one surgery and is calculating how long she can wait before her next patient is affected, and Gordon, a retired teacher who is quietly pleased that his schedule for the day consisted only of returning library books. Nadia pounds the emergency button every few minutes. Gordon reads the card on the back of the elevator door.
questions.text: How does the author contrast the two characters' points of view?
options: By showing that Nadia is more intelligent than Gordon and thus more aware of the danger
By using the same elevator setting to reveal that each character experiences the same situation through a completely different emotional lens
By having Gordon directly criticize Nadia's urgency, creating a central conflict
By describing Nadia's thoughts but only Gordon's actions, making her viewpoint more sympathetic
questions.explanation: The identical setting throws the characters' contrasting inner lives into sharp relief: Nadia's urgency versus Gordon's quiet ease shows how point of view is shaped by the stakes each person brings to the same moment.

questions.passage: The passenger pigeon was once the most abundant bird in North America, with flocks so large they darkened the sky for hours. Naturalist John James Audubon described one 1813 migration as lasting three days without interruption. Yet by 1914, the species was extinct. Hunting played a role, but ecologists now point to habitat destruction as the more decisive factor — the loss of the vast eastern forests that the birds required for nesting in the enormous communal colonies they depended on to reproduce successfully.
questions.text: Cite two pieces of textual evidence that support the idea that the passenger pigeon's extinction was surprising given its earlier abundance.
options: Audubon's three-day migration sighting and the fact that the species was gone within roughly a century
The role of hunting and the loss of eastern forests
The bird's dependence on communal nesting and the ecologists' current research
The darkening of the sky and the existence of habitat destruction laws
questions.explanation: The most direct evidence of the contrast between abundance and extinction is the sheer scale Audubon documented (a three-day flock) and the fact that such a population collapsed to zero within about a century.

questions.passage: Historians have long debated whether the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation or merely accelerated a movement that would have emerged anyway. What is beyond dispute is that Martin Luther's 95 Theses spread across Europe within weeks of being written — an unprecedented speed made possible by the press. Equally significant, the press produced vernacular Bibles, allowing ordinary people to read scripture without a priest's interpretation. These two effects — the rapid spread of dissenting ideas and the democratization of religious texts — fundamentally altered the relationship between individuals and religious institutions.
questions.text: What are the TWO central ideas of this passage?
options: The printing press caused the Reformation, and Martin Luther was its most important leader
The press spread dissenting ideas rapidly and democratized access to religious texts, both of which challenged institutional religious authority
Historians disagree about the Reformation, and vernacular Bibles were printed for the first time after Luther
The speed of printing changed communication, and religious institutions eventually adopted the new technology
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly names these two effects — rapid spread of dissent and democratization of religious reading — as the developments that 'fundamentally altered' the relationship with religious institutions.

questions.passage: In the 1850s, the American West was largely unmapped. The federal government commissioned surveys partly to support a transcontinental railroad and partly to assert territorial claims over land still occupied by Indigenous nations. The surveys produced detailed maps, but the act of mapping also transformed public perception — land that appeared on a government map seemed, to Eastern audiences, to belong to the nation rather than to its inhabitants. This perceptual shift made it easier for Congress to pass legislation opening mapped lands to settlement.
questions.text: How did the government surveys lead to the legislative outcomes described in the passage?
options: The surveys directly forced Indigenous people to leave their land
Surveys produced maps that shifted public perception of ownership, making it politically easier to pass settlement legislation
Congress commissioned the surveys specifically to create legal justification for removal laws
The detailed maps were used in court cases that established federal ownership of western territories
questions.explanation: The passage traces a cause-and-effect chain: surveys created maps, maps shifted perception of land ownership among Eastern audiences, and that perceptual shift made settlement legislation easier to pass.

questions.passage: The committee described the proposed policy as 'revenue-neutral,' meaning no additional taxes would be collected. Critics, however, argued that shifting the tax burden from higher-income brackets to consumption taxes was not neutral at all — it was, in their view, regressive, placing proportionally heavier costs on lower-income households who spend a greater share of their income on basic goods.
questions.text: What does the word 'regressive' mean as used in this passage?
options: Moving backward in time toward an earlier policy
Placing a proportionally greater burden on lower-income people
Reducing overall government revenue through tax cuts
Describing a policy that has been rejected and then reconsidered
questions.explanation: The passage defines the critics' use of 'regressive' in context: a tax that takes a larger proportional share from lower-income households because they spend more of their income on taxed goods.

questions.passage: The third paragraph of the article describes a single afternoon in a Nairobi medical clinic: a doctor, three nurses, and a line of patients stretching out the door. The paragraph uses no statistics. It records only what happens in two hours — the diagnoses made, the medicines dispensed, the one patient turned away because the supply of a critical drug had run out. The fourth paragraph then presents WHO data showing that 45% of sub-Saharan clinics face similar shortages monthly.
questions.text: Why does the author place the specific clinic scene before the statistical data?
options: To establish credibility by showing personal experience with the subject
To create an emotional, human-scale example that gives meaning to the statistics that follow
To argue that statistics alone cannot capture the complexity of health care systems
To introduce the doctor and nurses as central figures in the article's main argument
questions.explanation: Placing a concrete, human narrative before the broader statistical data is a structural choice that makes the abstract numbers emotionally meaningful — the reader sees the shortage in human terms before seeing its scale.

questions.passage: A wildlife biologist writes: 'The reintroduction of gray wolves to Yellowstone in 1995 has been an ecological success by nearly every measurable standard. Elk herds have become healthier and more mobile, riverside vegetation has recovered, and songbird populations have increased. Those who oppose wolf reintroduction typically represent ranching interests, and their concerns, while understandable, should not override a demonstrated conservation benefit shared by the entire public.'
questions.text: How does the author distinguish their position from opposing views?
options: By presenting the opposing ranching perspective in equal detail before refuting it
By characterizing opponents as representing narrow economic interests while framing wolf reintroduction as a broad public benefit
By citing peer-reviewed research that directly contradicts ranchers' claims about livestock losses
By acknowledging that both sides have equally valid scientific evidence
questions.explanation: The author identifies the opposing side with 'ranching interests' (a specific economic group) while framing support for wolves as a 'public' benefit — a rhetorical move that positions the author's view as broadly shared and the opposition as narrowly self-interested.

questions.text: Identify the function of the underlined phrase in this sentence: 'Running every morning, she gradually built her endurance.'
options: It is a prepositional phrase acting as an adverb
It is a participial phrase acting as an adjective modifying 'she'
It is a noun clause acting as the subject of the sentence
It is an infinitive phrase acting as a direct object
questions.explanation: 'Running every morning' is a participial phrase (beginning with the participle 'running') that modifies the subject 'she,' functioning as an adjective in the sentence.

questions.text: Which sentence is a compound-complex sentence?
options: She studied for the test.
She studied, and her brother read.
Although it was late, she studied, and her brother finally fell asleep.
Although it was late, she continued to study for the exam.
questions.explanation: A compound-complex sentence contains at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause. Option C has a dependent clause ('Although it was late') and two independent clauses ('she studied' and 'her brother finally fell asleep').

questions.text: Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?
options: Barking loudly, the dog scared the mail carrier.
The student turned in the essay that she had revised carefully.
Running down the street, the backpack fell off his shoulder.
The teacher handed back the tests that she had graded.
questions.explanation: In 'Running down the street, the backpack fell off his shoulder,' the participial phrase 'running down the street' is misplaced — it appears to modify 'backpack,' but backpacks do not run. The person was running, not the backpack.

questions.text: Which sentence correctly uses a comma to separate coordinate adjectives?
options: She wore a long, elegant, red gown.
She wore a long elegant red gown.
She wore a long, elegant gown.
She wore a long elegant, red gown.
questions.explanation: Coordinate adjectives independently modify the noun and should be separated by commas. 'Long' and 'elegant' are coordinate adjectives here. 'Red' is considered part of the noun phrase 'red gown' and does not take a preceding comma.

questions.text: Which revision makes the sentence more precise and concise? Original: 'Due to the fact that it was raining, we made the decision to cancel the outside event.'
options: Due to the fact that rain was occurring, we decided to cancel the outside event.
Because it was raining, we cancelled the outdoor event.
It was raining, and so a decision was made to cancel the event that was outside.
We decided that the event, which was outside, should be cancelled due to rain occurring.
questions.explanation: 'Due to the fact that' is a wordy phrase that can be replaced by 'because,' and 'made the decision to cancel' can be shortened to 'cancelled.' Option B is the most concise and precise revision.

questions.passage: The surgeon described the procedure as minimally invasive, assuring the patient that she would make only a small incision and that recovery time would be negligible compared to traditional open surgery. The patient, relieved, signed the consent form.
questions.text: Based on context, what does 'negligible' most likely mean?
options: Uncertain and difficult to predict
So small as to be hardly worth considering
Longer than average but manageable
Identical to recovery time from traditional surgery
questions.explanation: The surgeon uses 'negligible' to reassure the patient by comparing recovery favorably to traditional surgery, suggesting it is so short as to be barely worth worrying about.

questions.text: Read this sentence: 'The soldier made the ultimate sacrifice.' What figure of speech is 'ultimate sacrifice' in this context?
options: Hyperbole
Irony
Euphemism
Oxymoron
questions.explanation: A euphemism substitutes a mild or indirect expression for one that might seem harsh. 'Ultimate sacrifice' is a euphemism for dying in combat, softening the direct statement of death.

questions.text: Which sentence uses verbal irony?
options: After failing every question on the quiz, she said, 'Well, that went brilliantly.'
The thunder was so loud it shook the windows.
He was the tallest student in the school.
The wind whispered through the leaves.
questions.explanation: Verbal irony occurs when a speaker says the opposite of what they mean. Calling a complete failure 'brilliant' is sarcastic — the speaker means the opposite of what the words literally say.

questions.passage: The city council should reject the proposed sports arena. Construction will cost taxpayers \$400 million. Studies of comparable arenas in six other cities found that promised economic benefits — new jobs and increased tourism — consistently failed to materialize at the projected levels. Meanwhile, the same \$400 million could fund repairs to 200 public schools, directly benefiting 80,000 students who currently attend schools with leaking roofs and broken heating systems.
questions.text: Evaluate the strength of this argument.
options: Weak, because the author does not explain why economic benefits failed to materialize in other cities
Weak, because the author uses emotional language about children to distract from the economic argument
Strong, because it supports its central claim with specific data from comparable cases and offers a concrete alternative use of funds
Strong, because it proves the sports arena will have no economic benefit to the city
questions.explanation: The argument cites studies of six comparable cities (specific, relevant evidence), gives concrete numbers (\$400 million, 200 schools, 80,000 students), and proposes an alternative — all elements of a well-supported argument.
